Federal regulators crack down on organ donation groups
The Organ Transplant Service teams at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center started using robotic surgery for kidney transplants in 2018. Nationwide, more than 109,000 people are on waiting lists for organ procurement. (Photo courtesy of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center)
Federal regulators are cracking down on the nonprofits responsible for coordinating organ donations, aiming to begin shutting down substandard groups by early next year.
New criteria will score the organizations on donation and transplantation rates and will decertify the bottom tier, meaning their contracts with the federal government will be revoked. Many professional medical groups welcome more stringent evaluations. But the nonprofits strongly oppose aspects of the criteria and have filed lawsuits, warning of potential disruptions in some states or regions.
More than 109,000 people are on waiting lists nationwide for organ procurement, according to federal data as of July. The majority of patients await kidneys. Each day on average, about a dozen patients die waiting for an organ.
State- and region-based nonprofits known as organ procurement organizations recover organs from deceased donors and work with families and transplant centers to coordinate donations. The procurement organizations have faced heavy scrutiny in recent years, with media reports and research papers highlighting issues such as skipping over some transplant centers and sicker patients, which worsens racial and socioeconomic disparities in organ transplants.
The feds have shut down at least two groups in the past two years, citing questionable practices and saying that there were cases in which workers ignored signs of consciousness in donors.
Changes have been in the works for years. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services first announced the new evaluation framework in 2020, in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump. Earlier this year, CMS released proposed revisions to that rule.
Aiming for better accountability, transparency and oversight of the groups, as well as increasing patient protections and organ recovery, CMS will score the nation’s 55 organ procurement organizations based on their donation and transplantation rates.
It will rank them into three tiers: Top tier organizations — those calculated in the top 25% of organizations for donation and transplantation rates — would be automatically renewed for another four years. Those that fall in the second tier will have the opportunity to improve and reapply for certification, while those ranking in the bottom tier would be decertified entirely. Other nonprofits will then make bids to the federal government to take over their service areas, according to CMS.
The new evaluation method has stirred debate. Some medical and policy experts say better oversight of the nonprofits is long overdue, while organ procurement organizations say they will face logistical hurdles in coordinating lifesaving organs if some are shut down.
CMS hasn’t yet released which organization’s contracts will be renewed or dropped, but said in March that the process would begin sometime late this year. The current four-year contracts expire in January, but CMS has said it will issue extensions as needed to ensure organ transplants continue.

Missouri congressional map fight reaches voters as Republican campaign goes quiet
Proposition A will determine whether a map designed to give Republicans another U.S. House seat takes effect in 2028. But the fight could continue even if voters reject it
Supporters of a referendum on Missouri’s gerrymandered redistricting map rally at the state Capitol Building Tuesday, May 12 after the Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments on two cases involving the redistricting map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Missouri Republicans spent more than a year fighting to put a new congressional map into effect, including a costly campaign to prevent voters from having the final say.
Now that voters have that say, the organized Republican campaign to defend the map has all but vanished.
On Nov. 3, Missourians will decide Proposition A, a referendum on a redistricting plan passed last year at President Donald Trump’s urging to improve Republicans’ chances of winning seven of Missouri’s eight seats in the U.S. House. A “yes” vote approves the new map; a “no” vote rejects it and keeps the boundaries adopted in 2022.
Neither outcome will change the congressional districts used in this year’s election. After a prolonged legal fight, the U.S. Supreme Court ordered Missouri to use its 2022 map in November. Proposition A will instead determine which boundaries apply beginning with the 2028 election, barring another redistricting effort.
The campaign to defeat Proposition A is pouring money into advertising and voter outreach. People Not Politicians, which collected the signatures that forced the referendum, has reported $5.4 million in contributions of at least $5,000 each since mid September.
Put Missouri First, meanwhile, spent about $2.9 million trying to block the referendum but has reported no large donations since July.
Michael Hafner, a spokesman for Put Missouri First, said the hope is that “Missourians will tune out the noise and look beyond the millions of dollars in advertising” and support the map drawn by lawmakers last year.
“Prop A deserves Missourians’ support because it delivers a practical, commonsense map that respects more community boundaries throughout our state,” he told The Independent.
But while Republicans continue hoping voters will approve the map, Hafner told St. Louis Public Radio there is currently no organized effort to support the passage of Proposition A. Instead, the GOP is investing money and resources in other races.
“The left has allocated significant funds into defeating the map,” he said, “and Republicans nationally have other fish to fry.”
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who fought unsuccessfully to keep the referendum off the ballot, said he remains firmly behind the new congressional boundaries. He acknowledged the competition for campaign dollars and public attention but said he believes supporters of the map are organizing at the grassroots level.
“While they might not be the loudest or most well funded,” he said, “I believe they are a formidable force and their efforts will be worthwhile on election night.”

At the center of the dispute is Kansas City and the 5th Congressional District, represented since 2005 by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver.

Want to end redistricting wars? Start by uncapping the US House.
The U.S. Capitol on April 9 (Ashley Murray/States Newsroom).
Missouri’s congressional redistricting battle has taken voters on a dizzying tour of the court system leading up to the midterms. After trips to the Missouri Supreme Court and federal district court resulted in different rulings, the state took not one but two trips to the U.S. Supreme Court, which held – twice – that the state should use its 2022 congressional map for the November 2026 election. Voters will decide the fate of the new map through Proposition A.
The legal question that dominated these disputes was about whether Missouri could use a newly drawn map despite a valid referendum petition. But the process invokes a larger and more important question about our representation: why has control of a single congressional seat become so consequential that politicians are willing to fight over it in multiple court rooms instead of trusting voters to decide?
One way voters can take matters into their own hands is to support uncapping the U.S. House of Representatives. From our nation’s founding until the passage of the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, the House grew alongside the national population. The cap at 435 members created an artificial scarcityaround representation, and that scarcity is one of the drivers fueling the current gerrymandering wars, in Missouri and beyond.
With the same number of House seats representing a population that has more than tripled since 1929, each individual district has become larger, and political control of each one has become more consequential.
Missouri’s congressional delegation provides a particularly striking example. When the House was capped in 1929, Missouri had 16 seats in the House, representing a population of 3.6 million residents, or approximately 225,000 constituents per representative. By contrast, today Missouri has only eight House seats, representing a population of nearly 6.3 million, meaning that each representative has approximately 783,000 constituents. In other words, Missouri’s population has nearly doubled yet its House delegation has been cut in half.
The average Missourian now experiences a much lower quality of representation as a result, because even the most conscientious representatives struggle to serve such large districts. For example, Missouri’s 6thCongressional District, spanning all of northern Missouri from the Kansas border to the Mississippi River, includes 39 counties and is so large that it covers more square miles than nine U.S. states.
To be clear, uncapping the House is not a panacea for partisan gerrymandering. The process will always be political, and the parties will always compete to control the process. But expanding the House would reduce the artificial scarcity problem that has made each individual seat such an extraordinarily valuable political asset. More representation is also consistent with what the Founders intended – in Federalist No. 55, Madison warned against making the House too small, arguing that it must be large enough to secure “a full knowledge of the interest of its constituents,” and ensure “that its members are not lifted too far aloft from the mass of the citizens.”
Smaller districts would also mean more opportunities for voters to elect someone responsive to their communities and less political power concentrated in each individual seat.

Just because you run doesn’t necessarily mean that you’re up on running shoe innovation. In recent years, there have been notable improvements in propulsion and efficiency, thanks to additions like carbon-fiber plates, smart sensors, and midsoles that promise high energy return. What’s more important than these buzzy words is: How do the shoes feel?
After all, you can have footwear designed by rocket scientists, but if you’re uncomfortable with every step, your run will be a slog, no matter the distance. You want your shoe to make the ride feel soft, which is why the On Cloudsurfer 3 stands out over so many others.
On running shoes have always been distinguished by their trademark hollow pods— the “clouds” that are specifically engineered to help create a softer underfoot experience and give the brand its unmistakable look. In the Cloudsurfer 3, On’s CloudTec Phase™ allows those pods to compress in sequence, helping absorb impact and create a smoother transition from heel to toe. This isn’t just another update to On’s running shoe line. With breakthrough Swiss engineering working beneath every step, the Cloudsurfer 3 delivers the brand’s softest ride yet.
A Smooth, Versatile Ride
An option for everyday and recovery runs as well as longer training sessions, the Cloudsurfer 3 combines CloudTec® Phase with On’s brand-new SurrealTM Superfoam. According to the brand’s internal testing, the pairing provides 15.5 percent deeper compression—and therefore more impact absorption—than the superfoam alone. The result is a softer landing that can help daily miles feel easier on the legs, particularly over long distances.
According to the same internal testing, the Cloudsurfer 3 is also predicted to deliver a 9.9 percent improvement in smooth-ride sensation. That figure reflects the way the reimagined CloudTec® Phase orientation enhances the rolling motion of the foot, helping each step flow more naturally into the next from landing to toe-off.
You’re also getting a newly engineered mesh upper in the Cloudsurfer 3, which provides a secure fit that adapts to your foot while still offering breathability and support. That breathability helps keep heat and moisture from building up, reducing the conditions that can lead to chafing, blisters, and hot spots.
Even the cushioning around the collar and tongue has been updated, so you get a cloud-like feel as soon as you slip them on. It doesn’t hurt that the Cloudsurfer 3 looks cool, too.
Together, these innovations give runners what they want from an everyday shoe: a natural feel, reliable performance, and lasting comfort. The result is a smoother ride, whether you’re going long or heading out for a quick training run.
Why Comfort Matters
That softer feel is a big deal, considering a 2025 study found that runners who perceived their shoes as more cushioned had a lower risk of running-related injury. When a shoe feels right, you’re less likely to think about every step—or adjust the way you’re moving to compensate for discomfort. That allows you to settle into your natural stride and focus on the run itself.
Enjoyment is a major factor, too. Wearing a shoe like the Cloudsurfer 3, with its focus on cushioning, responsiveness, and comfort, can be key to unlocking your best run yet—and enjoying yourself along the way. When that happens, even a hard run can feel softer, mile after mile.

Runners often assume that “running builds strong legs,” but a better way to think about this is: “Running requires strong legs.”
If you want to run faster and more efficiently then hill repeats, speed workouts, and long runs will help—but doing leg exercises consistently will give you the edge you need to power up inclines, have a strong finishing kick, and end a long run feeling good.
Relying solely on running is a “less-than-optimal” training strategy that can eventually lead to injuries too, Dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Irvine, California, tells Runner’s World.
To gain those benefits from your strength training, plus stay healthy and pick up your pace, Miklaus developed the following leg day workout. Incorporate it into your current strength-training plan or pair it with an easy run. (New to strength training? Start with our bodyweight leg workout first.)

You will need a heavy set of dumbbells and a loaded barbell. (If you don’t have a barbell, stick with the heavy dumbbells.) While you’ll want to start with lighter weights to get the form down, make sure to work up in weight. And don’t be afraid to go heavy: “Choose weights that are so heavy you literally cannot complete more than the prescribed reps,” Miklaus advises. “If you can do more at the end of the set, it’s not heavy enough.”

1. Stiff-Leg Deadlift
Why it works: The stiff-leg deadlift targets the hamstrings, glutes, and posterior core muscles, all of which tend to be neglected by runners who don’t strength train, Miklaus says. “This can lead to knee and hip injuries and decrease top speed,” he says. “Stiff-leg deadlifts help increase strength in those areas and can improve the power and speed of a runner’s ‘kick.’”
How to do it:
- Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a barbell in front of thighs with straight arms and an overhand or mixed grip.

- Repeat.

Why it works: Besides strengthening the posterior chain, dumbbell swings help develop a dynamic hip extension, which drives a runner’s forward propulsion.

On October 20, Wells Fargo released a study of affluent families that every parent with an estate plan should read.
Based on a survey of 800 Baby Boomers and 800 Gen X or Millennial children, the researchers found that 61% of adult children said inheritance had already caused problems in their families, from hurt feelings and arguments over fairness to estrangement and legal disputes. Only 29% of older parents said the same. Among the adult children, 49% believed inheritance conversations have the potential to trigger family conflict—which is one reason so many people avoid having them.
My book, Unspeakable, came out the same day as the survey, and that data provided an illustration of the book's core idea in the book: Many families are avoiding conversations because they're afraid of discomfort, even if this avoidance can cause harm. Estate planning is just one of the topics I cover in Unspeakable, but as I've traveled to give talks and answer questions about the book, it's one that's coming up most frequently.
In my work advising family businesses, I see this avoidance in various forms. In many cases, older parents hire my firm to help them inform their children about their estate plans. This is complicated work, but I find it fulfilling because I believe that in most cases, relationships become better when financial secrets are brought out into the open.
To help illustrate this, let me tell you about my work with a couple I'll call Jose and Natalia.
Born and raised in Latin America, Jose was educated as an accountant and worked for investment banks before founding a wildly successful private equity firm. The couple, who now live in San Francisco and are in their eighties, have built substantial wealth. Their assets total over $1 billion.
They have four children in their fifties, all well-educated and financially independent. Years ago the parents gave each child a significant gift—about $25 million each. The family had never discussed the provisions of Jose and Natalia's will, but the children have always assumed they would inherit most of the estate when the parents die.
Here's the secret: They won't. The children will be given lifetime use of the family's home, which are to be placed in a trust with maintenance funds. But everything else will be used to fund a charitable foundation devoted to mental health and education programs, run by an outside adviser. Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle each fell more than 2% that day. Revenue came in just 0.7% above analysts’ estimates and earnings per share topped expectations by 2.2%. With a beat this small, the more telling changes sit further down the report.
So where did IBM’s quarter actually turn?
IBM’s Software Business Sped Back Up
The turn came in software, which generated 44.4% of IBM’s revenue in fiscal 2025, more than any other segment. Management said software revenue growth jumped four points from the second quarter to reach 9%. It also said the division led a broader pickup across IBM’s segments, with infrastructure growth rising to 5%.
Management said the biggest difference came from a single part of the software business. On the October 21 call, executives explained that transactional sales, the software IBM sells in individual deals rather than as recurring revenue, make up about 20% of the software book. These sales fell by double digits in the second quarter, taking 4 to 5 points off software growth. In the third quarter, they rose by double digits. This swing was larger than software’s four-point pickup. Management also said its automation business faced a tougher comparison.
How Much Of IBM’s Software Jump Was Catch-Up?
Management said about a quarter of the jump came from large deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters was new business. For transaction processing, its mainframe software, management said the deferred second-quarter deals landed on top of a normal third-quarter mainframe buying cycle.
For IBM as a whole, the quarter looks more like a recovery from the second quarter than a step up. Total reported revenue grew 4.7% from a year earlier, an improvement from 1.1% in the second quarter. That pace still trails the first quarter, when revenue grew 9.5%.
What Does IBM Now Expect For 2026?
Management held its forecast for 2026 revenue growth at 4% to 5% at constant currency, the same range it gave in July. The company also raised its forecast for the year’s increase in free cash flow to more than $1 billion. For the software division, management now expects full-year growth of about 7% to 8%.
Management also expects part of the quarter’s strength to fade. Transaction processing, IBM’s mainframe software, grew 10% in the quarter. Executives do not expect that double-digit pace to continue, noting that growth might moderate from the third quarter into the fourth. While Red Hat bookings grew in the high teens, and management said such bookings growth turns into good revenue growth, the company did not want to comment on 2027 growth. It said it would quantify its view in January.
IBM’s full-year 2026 software growth, measured against management’s forecast of about 7% to 8%, is the figure to watch when the company reports in January 2027.

Tropical Cyclone Arnab is expected to hit India’s east coast on Wednesday, marking a break in an otherwise calm season that’s been subdued by a severe El Niño.
Arnab is currently 859 kilometers (534 miles) southwest of Kolkata, packing top sustained winds of 213 kilometers per hour, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center, equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane. The cyclone is forecast to intensify further before making landfall, though models are currently split on whether it will stall before or after crossing the coast, the center said.
El Niño has upended typical cyclone seasons around the world this year. The Atlantic Ocean is set for one of its lowest hurricane counts since 1941, while the Northwest Pacific Ocean is on track for one of its most intense typhoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, the North Indian Ocean has seen significantly below-average activity in recent months, with Arnab the first cyclonic storm.
“One of the key climatic events has been the suppression of the Indian monsoon and with it, the much reduced tropical cyclone activity, driven by the long reach of the El Niño,” said Christian Werner, managing director of Global Weather Climate Analytics.
Arnab is expected to bring moderate to intense rainfall across parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, and could cause widespread damage to standing crops and plantations including banana, papaya, and drumstick trees, according to the India Meteorological Department. Deluges over Nepal, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka are also possible, forecasts show.
The North Indian Ocean sees storm activity peak during two distinct periods of the year: before the monsoon, from April to June, and after the monsoon, from October to December.

Voters line up outside Shiloh Hills Baptist Church in Kennesaw, Georgia, on Election Day, May 19, 2026. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors to every state ahead of Election Day, expanding a longstanding practice that’s spurred concern this year among Democrats and voting rights advocates because of President Donald Trump’s push to influence elections.
The Justice Department for decades has deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process. During President Joe Biden’s administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections.
The 2026 monitoring program is larger, with the Justice Department announcing it will have a presence in all 50 states. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday that about 1,000 monitors will be involved but that the department won’t disclose the full list of monitored locations until Election Day — Nov. 3.
“Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day,” Pels said in a statement.
Lawsuits prompt unease
While election monitors, who watch polling places and election officials for compliance with federal voting rights laws, have long been a feature of U.S. elections, the Trump administration’s extraordinary moves to assert federal authority over state-run elections have left many Democrats and even some Republicans uneasy about this year’s expansive effort.
The Justice Department has sued dozens of states in an attempt to force election officials to turn over voter lists that contain sensitive personal data, such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The DOJ has lost 27 cases so far, and won none.
Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department sued California to block election officials from counting ballots from roughly 20,000 voters it says are suspected noncitizens.
And on Friday, the DOJ sued Alaska to preemptively prevent the certification of its U.S. Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses by less than the number of votes received by another candidate of the same name, citing the potential for voter confusion.
But concerns about DOJ monitors began building in August after Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, expressed reservations about monitors, calling their actions “very odd” after DOJ personnel watched voting in the state’s primary election.
Andrew Walchuk, senior policy director and counsel for voting & fair representation at the watchdog group Common Cause, told reporters last month that monitors in and of themselves are nothing new, pointing to the long history of the DOJ’s monitoring program.
“But with this administration, we will be watching their activity very closely,” Walchuk said.

The percentage of people without health insurance is growing
Dr. Navdeep Lehga sets up equipment in the exam room of a mobile clinic in Mendota, California in 2025. The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has grown in the past two years, according to a new report. (Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local)
The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has increased in the past two years, largely because many people can no longer afford Obamacare coverage after Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year.
The uninsured rate for adults ages 19-64 rose to 11.2% this year, up from 8.9% in 2024, according to a new analysis by the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy and philanthropic nonprofit.
Nearly half of the 7,362 working-age adults who participated in the group’s biennial health insurance survey said they were uninsured, underinsured, or experienced a gap in coverage this year. Half said they delayed or avoided getting medical care because of the cost, compared with 46% in 2022.
The subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But the aid was designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and Congress allowed it to expire at the end of last year.
As a result, the percentage of working-age adults with health insurance from the marketplaces created under Obamacare, officially known as the Affordable Care Act, declined to 6% this year, from 8% in 2024.
The percentage of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid also declined, to 13% this year from 16% in 2022, as many states removed people from the rolls at the conclusion of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The increase in the uninsured rate almost certainly will accelerate in January, when the Republican tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act takes effect. That law will require many Medicaid recipients to prove they are working or engaging in approved community service activities for at least 80 hours a month.
The law also mandates that states verify enrollees’ Medicaid eligibility every six months.
Another factor in the growing percentage of people without coverage is the rising cost of healthcare, which is pushing up premiums for private insurance.
“It’s affecting people’s ability to pay off bills right away, and it’s having an effect on health plans,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund and the lead author of the report.
Almost a third of the survey respondents, whether insured and uninsured, said they currently had medical or dental bills or were paying off medical debt. And more than 70% of uninsured adults said they had cost-related problems getting care.
“I think it’s very concerning,” Collins said. “We know from our survey data that not going to get care isn’t and just generally is not good for people’s health over the long run.”
The rise in the uninsured rate comes after a long period of progress: Between 2010 and 2025, the overall uninsured rate in the United States fell by half, to 8% from nearly 16%, largely because of the Affordable Care Act.

The Western District Court of Appeals found that a man resentenced in 2023 must receive credit for time served on all four concurrent sentences
Deandre Pointer, serving four concurrent 23-year-sentences in the Missouri Department of Corrections, won a ruling Tuesday that he must get credit for all time he has served on all four counts of his conviction. If he had lost, Pointer would have been incarcerated for 40 years. He is shown in a 2025 interview (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
A Missouri man who should have been eligible for release in 2024 remains in prison because the state miscalculated his credit for time he had already served, the Missouri Western District Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday.
Deandre Pointer was sentenced to 23 years in the Department of Corrections on four counts, two of second-degree murder and two of armed criminal action, with the sentences to run concurrently. He received the sentence in 2023 after a Jackson County judge determined Pointer was abandoned by his public defender in a post-conviction case filed after his original sentence was handed down in 2005.
When the resentencing was finished, Pointer thought he would be out in about a year, when he had served the required 85% of the sentence. But when a Missouri Department of Corrections record clerk finished processing his paperwork, his projected release date was 2044.
The department misapplied the law on how to calculate his sentence, Judge Alok Ahuja wrote in the court’s unanimous opinion.
“The Missouri Supreme Court has held that, ‘in construing (state law), we are guided by the principle that criminal statutes must be ‘construed strictly against the (s)tate and liberally in favor of the defendant,’” Ahuja wrote.
The 2023 resentencing changed both the charge in one count, from first- to second-degree murder, and the way the sentences were imposed, from consecutive to concurrent.
“Pointer’s conviction and sentence for first-degree murder on Count 1 must be treated as if they never occurred,” Ahuja wrote.
In a 2025 interview with The Independent, Pointer said he pursued a new sentence because he was a victim of crime, forced to help the perpetrator out of fear for his own safety.
The stress of having to fight for release after winning his resentencing has taken a severe toll, he said at the time.

“I never took anxiety meds,” Pointer said. “Never in my life. Now, you know, I have to take anxiety meds just to have a functional day.”

The Western District decision overturned a February ruling from Cole County Circuit Judge Brian Stumpe that found the department had calculated the sentence correctly.

Mark Kiptoo has had some pretty memorable trips to Frankfurt. He won the city's marathon in 2014, returned four years later to set a then-world record for runners over 40, and on Sunday added another achievement to the list. This time, at 50 years old.
The Kenyan distance runner finished the Frankfurt Marathon on October 25 in 2:15:24, averaging roughly 5:10 per mile across 26.2 miles. He placed 13th overall, but his performance was particularly impressive for another reason: It was the fastest marathon ever recorded by a man in the 50–54 age group—and it wasn't especially close.
For 35 years, the M50 record belonged to South Africa's Titus Mamabolo, who ran 2:19:29 in Durban in July 1991. Kiptoo cut four minutes and five seconds off that mark on Sunday, a substantial improvement that now awaits official ratification by World Masters Athletics.
Kiptoo has barely had time to get used to being 50. He celebrated his birthday on June 21, less than two months after finishing 2:12:21 at the Geneva Marathon. That performance came too early to qualify for an M50 record, but it offered a pretty good preview of what he could do once he entered the age group.
Frankfurt wasn't even his first record-setting performance this month. On October 4, Kiptoo won the San Sebastián Half Marathon in Spain in 1:03:57, establishing a new M50 world-best time for the distance. Three weeks later, he was back on a starting line, this time with twice as many miles to cover.
Kiptoo didn't start competing until he was 28, entering his first race in 2004 while serving in the Kenyan Air Force. He went on to win the African 5,000-meter title in 2012, but didn't make his marathon debut until age 37. That first 26.2 was in Frankfurt, where he finished second in 2013, just one second behind the winner.
He also lost roughly a year of training to Achilles tendon trouble and the pandemic, according to the Frankfurt organizers. He returned to win the Zurich Marathon three years in a row from 2023 through 2025, clocking 2:09:16 in his last victory at age 48.
Before Sunday's race, Kiptoo told organizers he hoped his running would inspire people not to give up or stop taking care of their bodies as they got older. Running a 2:15 marathon at 50 certainly gives him a pretty persuasive example to point to.

Wells Fargo and Merrill Agree to Pay $4.4 Million Over Small Stock Trades. What Happens When Retirement Investors Pay Too Much to Trade?
State regulators just forced two major brokerages to pay back millions in commissions their customers never knew they were losing. The same quiet erosion could be happening inside your 401(k) right now.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Small stock trades aren’t always cheap ones. On Oct. 15, state securities regulators announced a $4.4 million settlement involving two Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC | WFC Price Prediction) brokerage units and Merrill Lynch, part of Bank of America (NYSE: BAC). The North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) said the firms had charged unreasonable commissions on thousands of small-dollar stock trades.
What Regulators Found on 256,000 Small Trades
Massachusetts regulators led a multistate investigation that uncovered unreasonable commissions on more than 256,000 stock trades over five years. The problem was minimum commissions, which can turn even a modest transaction into an expensive one.
The two Wells Fargo units collected nearly $3.9 million in unreasonable commissions across approximately 228,243 trades between Sept. 30, 2020, and Oct. 1, 2025. Merrill Lynch accounted for another $549,000 in excessive charges during the same period.
Affected customers in participating states will receive refunds plus interest, and the firms must certify that they’ve changed their commission practices. The investigation concerned retail brokerage accounts, not specifically 401(k)s. But workplace retirement investors can face trading commissions through brokerage windows, along with fund expenses and other charges that quietly eat into their savings.
A $250,000 Balance and a Fee Nobody Noticed
Picture a hypothetical 55-year-old with $250,000 in his 401(k). He never sees a separate bill for investment expenses, so he assumes his plan costs him nothing. But his funds and plan charges run an extra 0.5 percentage point a year compared with similar, lower-cost options.
On his current balance, that difference amounts to roughly $1,250 in one year, assuming the balance doesn’t change.
Now stretch the comparison over a decade. Suppose the cheaper portfolio earns 6% annually after fees, while the more expensive one earns 5.5%. With no additional contributions, his $250,000 would grow to approximately $447,700 in the cheaper option, compared with $427,000 in the pricier one.
That’s a difference of nearly $20,700 from an additional half-percentage-point in annual costs, compounded over 10 years.
Four Places 401(k) Costs Hide
- Fund expense ratios. These expenses are built into the fund’s returns rather than billed separately on your statement. You can find them in your plan’s investment disclosures and fund documents, but it’s easy to overlook their effect on your balance.
- Administrative and recordkeeping fees. These pay for running the plan: recordkeeping, legal work and the website. Some plans charge a flat dollar amount and others take a percentage of assets. When they come out of your account, they show up on your statements.
- Managed account or advice fees. A 2025 NEPC survey found that 46% of participating retirement plan sponsors offered managed accounts. These services may charge an additional asset-based fee on top of the expenses of the underlying investments.

The tech sector’s resistance to tokenized stocks keeps building.
Intel, Oracle, IBM, and quantum computing firm IonQ are the latest companies to object to having their shares traded on OKXICE TSV, according to an updated public notice from the venue dated Monday.
The planned platform, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, now lists 26 objecting issuers.
That’s up from 22 in its Oct. 23 notice, which added Wells Fargo, Cisco, and Marvell. The tally stood at 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15, when the first batch included Verizon, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group. In less than two weeks, the list has nearly tripled.
Technology companies dominate the roster. Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Arm, Cisco, and now Intel and Oracle have all objected, along with banks Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo.
IBM and IonQ add two quantum computing players. As before, the notices don’t explain the companies’ reasons or what an objection means for whether a stock can trade on the platform.
OKXICE TSV plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.
Users must pass identity and sanctions checks and hold a nontransferable “soulbound” token to trade. The venue is set to operate under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.
The latest notice highlights a key risk for investors. Each token represents a claim on a real share held by a third-party “tokenizer” through a registered broker-dealer. If that broker-dealer failed, the notice says, it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in a self-custodied wallet would count as customer property or be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which protects brokerage customers when firms fail.
The notice also says trades must be fully funded, with no margin or borrowing. Liquidity providers don’t have to be registered market makers and can pull their liquidity at any time.

Banks that keep outside AI agents out of customer accounts are guarding their own revenue rather than their customers, Bianco Research president Jim Bianco said on Unchained’s Bits + Bips during a live stream on Oct. 26.
“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?” he asked.
His example was JPMorgan Chase, which keeps third-party AI agents from signing in to Chase accounts or acting on them for customers. Jamie Dimon, the bank’s CEO, explained the policy to analysts on Oct. 13, warning of “rogue agents” and saying JPMorgan is “not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company” because that is “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.” A spokesperson told Fortune that “protecting our customers is our top priority,” adding, “We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers.”
Citi, Bank of America and Wells Fargo have taken steps to limit third-party agents as well, and Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster has said the brokerage is shutting out third-party agents that try to move funds in customer accounts. Wells Fargo’s revised online access agreement, which takes effect Nov. 24, says transactions by an AI agent a customer authorizes are treated as the customer’s own, and makes the customer responsible for the agent’s unintended actions until the customer tells the bank it has revoked the agent’s access.

A Model Built on Friction
Bianco said the traditional finance “business model is based on laziness.” Customers don’t want to log in every day to move idle cash into a money market fund, he said, but an agent could do it for them. In his account, banks profit by investing deposits that pay the customer nothing. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.
He put the money sitting in “zero-yielding bank accounts” at $4 trillion. Noninterest-bearing deposits in the domestic offices of U.S. banks came to about $4.04 trillion at the end of June, roughly 21% of domestic deposits, according to the FDIC’s Quarterly Banking Profile. Bianco predicted that customers would press for access anyway, noting that people already trade away their privacy online. “I think the public is gonna start demanding more and more of this,” he said.
Co-host Ram Ahluwalia, founder and CEO of Lumida Wealth Management, agreed on the motive. “They’re protecting themselves,” he said on the stream, adding that “the agents here are acting as fiduciaries of the customer.” He cautioned against overstating the risk of agent-driven deposit flight, though, since frictions such as opening a new bank account remain.

Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled "Protecting your finances in the Al World," Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, "including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf."
You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular. This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers' money. As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.

Customer satisfaction with total loss auto insurance claims fell for a third straight year, while satisfaction improved for claims involving repairable vehicles, a new study looking at this year shows.
Customer satisfaction with total loss claims fell 12 points on a 1,000-point scale in 2026, marking a 46-point decline since 2023, according to the JD Power 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study.
However, satisfaction with claims involving repairable vehicles improved four points and overall auto claims customer satisfaction was unchanged from last year at 700.
Overall, 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses this year, up from 16% four years ago. The growing share of total losses reflects rising vehicle repair costs, consumers keeping vehicles longer and higher deductibles removing smaller repairs from the claims process, according to the study. Affordability pressures also led some customers to drop rental coverage or increase deductibles, complicating the claims experience.
Repair cycle times have improved as claim volumes have declined and repair shops have more capacity. Average repair cycle times fell to 15.3 days in the first quarter of 2026, down 10 days from the first quarter of 2024, the study shows.
The study also found differences in customer satisfaction based on how effectively insurers communicate across channels. Satisfaction averaged 804 among customers who strongly agreed their insurers provided a seamless experience across communication channels, compared with 390 among customers who disagreed.
The study shows that insurers provided a seamless cross-channel experience 54% of the time, one of the lowest-performing measures in the study. Problems cited included unclear explanations, customers having to use multiple channels to get answers and digital tools that did not work as expected.
Amica ranked highest in overall customer satisfaction with a score of 775, followed by Nationwide at 743 and Automobile Club of Southern California (AAA) at 740.
The study examines auto claims experiences in order of importance: trust, fairness of settlement, people, time to settle claim, communication, ease of resolving claim, ease of starting claim and digital channels. The 2026 study was based on responses from 8,261 auto insurance customers who settled claims within the nine months before participating in the survey, which was conducted from September 2025 through August 2026.

Verisk tried to pull out of the deal last December after the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notified it that it had not completed its review of the transaction by the termination date of December 26. AccuLynx went to court to force Verisk to complete the deal.
Verisk had announced its plan to acquire AccuLynx in July 2025 and initially said it expected to close by the third quarter of 2025. AccuLynx and Verisk believed that the merger presented only minimal antitrust risk, as the companies did not compete horizontally or have a vertical supplier-customer relationship.
After last week’s Delaware Supreme Court ruling, Verisk said that it would comply with the ruling but cannot guarantee that the merger will be finalized.
Acculynx objected to Verisk’s exit from their agreement, claiming Verisk was responsible for the FTC delay that it then tried to use to walk away from their merger agreement.
In August, Chancery Court Judge Bonnie David agreed with AccuLynx. The judge found that Verisk’s termination was invalid because Verisk’s own “willful conduct caused the failure of a condition to closing.”
Verisk had answered no when the FTC first asked whether Verisk had ever terminated integration discussions with an AccuLynx competitor or rejected a request for an enhanced integration. The FTC had information that Verisk had in fact done so with a company called ServiceTitan. So the FTC asked again and as a result of having to issue a second request told Verisk it could not meet a December 26 deadline for review. Days later, Verisk purported to terminate the merger agreement on the extended termination date.
Acculynx asked the court to order Verisk to honor the merger agreement, including by using reasonable efforts to obtain clearance by the FTC and to close the merger if the FTC approves the transaction. AccuLynx also asked for damages in the amount of $3.85 million, plus prejudgment interest.
The Chancery Court ruled that AccuLynx was entitled to the order of specific performance against Verisk. The court also approved the damages for AccuLynx, finding that Verisk had waived its right to oppose the damages.
The court noted that the parties specifically agreed in the merger agreement that a party could not terminate if its own “willful conduct” was the “primary cause” of the failure to satisfy a condition. “It is not inequitable to hold the parties to their bargain,” the judge stated.
Verisk objected to the performance order requiring it to pursue the deal, arguing in part that such a remedy was not available where damages would provide adequate relief.
However, the Chancery Court noted that in addition to any other rights and remedies, the merger agreement made it clear that AccuLynx as seller had the right to enforce the obligations of the buyer “not only by an action or actions for damages but also by an action or actions for specific performance, injunctive and/or other equitable relief.”
The judge directed the parties to submit a proposed form of final order to implement the ruling.
The Delaware Supreme Court did not elaborate beyond saying that the Chancery Court opinion should be affirmed on the basis of and for the reasons stated.

A lawsuit filed on Friday involving the pay practices of Chili’s operator Brinker International is seeking to strike down New York state’s lower minimum wage for workers who earn tips, which it claims fuels the sexual and racial harassment of workers.
The proposed class action in federal court in Brooklyn by three former Chili’s employees claims that New York’s policy, which most other US states share, allows Brinker to force employees to rely on tips and exposes them to unlawful discrimination.
“Brinker promotes a culture in which tipped service employees make customers ‘feel special,’ even at the expense of their dignity and safety,” the lawsuit says.
Brinker did not respond to a request for comment. The New York Attorney General’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the challenge to the state law.
Many worker advocates have for years called for the elimination of sub-minimum wages that companies may pay to workers who earn tips under federal and most state laws, as long as tips make up the difference.
In New York, where the minimum wage is $16 an hour or $17 in and around New York City, food service workers who earn tips may be paid $10.70 or $11.35 an hour. The federal tipped minimum wage is $2.13 an hour, compared with the traditional minimum wage of $7.25, and applies in states that do not set their own minimums.
RELYING ON TIPS
Advocates say that because tips are discretionary and unpredictable, they should supplement workers’ incomes rather than make up most of their pay. The lawsuit against Brinker says that relying on tips forces workers to tolerate conduct such as sexual harassment and customers’ potential racial bias.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said in the lawsuit that they plan to expand the case to include a nationwide class of Chili’s workers.
Brinker operates more than 1,200 Chili’s restaurants in the US, including 36 in New York. The company also owns Maggiano’s Little Italy, an Italian restaurant chain with about 50 US locations.
The lawsuit claims that Chili’s reliance on customer ratings to determine workers’ schedules, shifts and table assignments is also unlawful. The ratings system can be racially biased, the lawsuit says, and can make it difficult for servers to reject unwanted advances from customers for fear of a poor rating.
The named plaintiffs, three former employees at a Chili’s in the Glendale section of Queens in New York City, claim they were routinely subjected to sexual advances and inappropriate comments and that management did not adequately protect workers from harassment.
(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rod Nickel)

A Washington contractor was fined $48,803 after a roofer was killed when he fell through a skylight.
Leslie & Campbell Inc. of Union Gap was fined $48,803 after a roofer fell more than 25 feet through an unguarded skylight to the concrete floor of a fruit packing warehouse in Wapato, according to the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries.
L&I cited the company after investigators found it had not guarded the skylight, identified skylights as a fall hazard or adequately trained workers on the danger.
The company is appealing the citation and fine.
L&I also issued penalties against other roofing companies and subcontractors in recent months:
- Roof Doctor Inc. of Olympia received the largest fine, $238,680, on June 30 for four willful serious and two serious fall protection violations. A portion of a roof collapsed beneath a worker in Tumwater, and inspectors determined his safety rope was too long to arrest his fall. The worker was hospitalized. Roof Doctor and its associated companies have been cited for more than 80 safety violations since 2004, including 34 for failing to ensure workers wore fall protection, according to L&I. The business is appealing the latest citation.
- Dabella/Reve Exteriors LLC of Marysville was fined $176,580 on Aug. 19 for two willful serious violations involving failure to protect subcontractor employees from falls and ensure they wore required protective equipment. Some violations repeated findings from earlier inspections, according to L&I. The company is appealing. Its subcontractor on the same job, Suruka House LLC, was fined $34,668 for repeatedly failing to ensure workers wore fall protection and other required protective equipment.
- Bartlett Homes & Roofing LLC of Veradale was fined $179,964 on June 3 for willful serious and repeat serious violations. Inspectors found two workers were not connected to a fall protection system, anchors were improperly installed and one worker’s fall restraint rope had enough slack that it would not have prevented him from hitting the ground. The company is appealing. Ivan’s Roofing Spokane LLC, a subcontractor on the same job, was fined $37,415 for workers not using fall protection, unsafe ladder use and failure to ensure first aid was available to injured workers.
- Money collected from fines goes into the workers’ compensation supplemental pension fund, which is earmarked to help injured workers and families of workers who died on the job.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the hot topic on Wall Street and Main Street right now. But for those old enough to remember, the environment may be starting to feel like the dot-com bubble, which burst at the turn of the century. Companies like Oklo (OKLO +5.36%), NuScale Power (SMR +8.16%), and even Constellation Energy (CEG +2.57%) all fell around 7% from their highs over the last five days, as of this writing. Bloom Energy (BE +7.15%) is down 13% from its high in that shockingly short period.
Meanwhile, ExxonMobil (XOM -2.51%) and Chevron (CVX -1.63%) are hitting all-time highs. There's risk in all of these stocks, but I'd rather own the stocks where the risks are easier to see and understand. That means Exxon and Chevron would be my pick. Here's why.
What happens when the AI bubble bursts?
The capital spending going into artificial intelligence is massive. AI is just a computer program, so it needs electricity to operate. That should lead to strong demand for power. That's the basic story behind companies like Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy.
Of the four, Oklo and NuScale are the most speculative. These two companies are attempting to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors. The opportunity could be huge, but at this point both companies are losing money and haven't yet proven their technologies are financially viable. Only the most aggressive investors should be considering them.

Bloom Energy and Constellation Energy have established and profitable businesses. Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells that provide off-grid power to AI data centers. Constellation Energy is an independent power producer selling power to the tech companies building out their AI operations. Bloom is the more aggressive option, as investors have priced a lot of good news into the stock. Even after a material pullback, the price-to-earnings ratio is still over 100x. Constellation Energy is probably the best positioned to weather an AI pullback, given the long-term contracts it signs, but irrational investors tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater when things turn south. If the AI bubble bursts, all of these stocks are likely to be hard hit, and the pullback over the last week is a sign of the all-or-nothing approach investors often take with new technologies.
Exxon and Chevron are built to survive

Procter & Gamble Held Profit Forecast As Costs Rose
Management kept its fiscal 2027 forecast for core earnings per share, the company’s adjusted measure, at $6.89 to $7.11, the same range it gave in July. The company held this outlook while raising its estimate of the hit from input costs, currency and items below operating profit to about 11% of fiscal 2026 core earnings per share, up from 8% in July. Even so, organic sales rose 4.0%, above the 1% to 3% organic growth P&G forecasts for the full year. Each of its 10 product categories grew.
The stock’s jump was not P&G’s alone. Over the same session, Colgate-Palmolive rose 4.3% and Church & Dwight 3.7%. Much of the day’s gain was shared with other household-goods makers, though P&G rose more than either.

Nvidia is the company best known for artificial intelligence (AI) chips, and that's because its graphics processing units (GPUs) have powered the training of the world's top models. And as a result, earnings have soared. But a quieter chip story is unfolding at Alphabet (GOOG +0.84%)(GOOGL +1.19%), and investors may just begin to see it in the company's financial results.
Alphabet has spent years designing its own AI chips, known as tensor processing units, or TPUs. For most of that time, these chips mainly served Google's own products and its cloud customers. This year, though, Alphabet started selling TPU systems directly to customers who want to run them in their own data centers.
So, why might the TPU be Alphabet's quietest advantage? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
From AI worry to AI winner
First, a quick look at how Alphabet got here. Not long ago, some investors worried the company would be a casualty of the AI era, with the idea that chatbots would pull users away from Google Search -- if that happened, it would clearly hurt advertising, which is Alphabet's bread and butter. Those worries haven't played out. In the second quarter, Google Search revenue grew 17%, and Google advertising represented 68% of total revenue.
Meanwhile, Google Cloud, the company's cloud computing arm, has been picking up serious momentum, with revenue advancing 63% in the first quarter and then 82% in the second, to reach more than $24 billion. And the cloud backlog, which represents contracted commitments not yet recognized as revenue, hit $514 billion, with just over half expected to convert to revenue within 24 months.
Where the TPU fits in
Here's where the chip comes in. Unlike a general-purpose chip, a TPU is designed with AI workloads in mind, and Alphabet has refined the technology across multiple generations. That gives the company two potential benefits. First, it can run its own AI services and those of its cloud customers on hardware it controls, rather than relying solely on Nvidia's supply and pricing. Second, it can now sell that hardware as a product.

Justin Stoneman has been in the trucking industry for 27 years, operating out of central Michigan’s agricultural heartland. Hauling grain and fertilizer around the Midwest, his 12-odd tractor trailers generated more than $3 million in annual revenue during their best times.
Those days are over. In the past year, Stoneman’s business has been squeezed by a range of pressures, from war-fueled spikes in diesel prices to rising insurance costs and onerous debts — all of which have pushed him to the brink. In May, his company, Stoneman Trucking LLC, filed for bankruptcy protection, but he has since lost hope and is shifting to chapter 7, to fully shut down operations.
“I’m so frustrated,” Stoneman said. “It’s like, what about all this ‘Drill, baby, drill’?”
Stoneman isn’t alone. At a time when affordability issues are at the center of US voters’ concerns heading into next week’s midterm elections, America’s smaller trucking operators are feeling the pinch. Some 221 trucking companies have filed for bankruptcy so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, extending a three-year spike at sustained levels not seen in decades.
Around two-thirds of small US carriers — typically operating 20 or fewer tractors, and oftentimes only just one — report that revenue is either flat or down compared with the year-ago period, according to a survey of hundreds of such companies conducted over the past two months by freight-management firm Truckstop and Bloomberg Intelligence. Almost 40% of these operators said that in six months, they expected to be out of trucking or weren’t sure where they’d be.
Chip Lane, managing partner at the bankruptcy-focused Lane Law Firm in Texas, said he’s seen a “massive uptick” in trucking companies approaching his firm to explore restructuring, sometimes as many as three or four in a week. “They are one of the top businesses that we see over and over and over again.”
It’s a function in part of the economics of getting in on the ground floor in trucking. Smaller operators typically begin as drivers for larger companies, then foster contacts and a reputation to strike out on their own, said Lane. But many don’t have the cash to buy a rig outright and often rely heavily on credit. This makes them more vulnerable than industry leaders like J.B. A high-speed rail service slammed into another train about 60 miles south of Madrid on Wednesday, killing at least 64 people — the second major accident on Spain’s rail network this year and the deadliest crash in over a decade.
“We’re talking about an enormous death toll,” said Emiliano García Page, president of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the accident occurred. “Firefighters expect that more victims will still be found.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is traveling to the area as evacuation efforts continue.
The crash has become Spain’s most lethal railway catastrophe since 2013, when 80 people perished after a train derailed in the Galicia region, north of Madrid. Another collision this past January also killed more than 40 people, provoking intense scrutiny of Spain’s rail infrastructure — once seen as a point of national pride.
Both accidents this year happened on the line running south from Madrid and involved state-owned train operator Renfe and Iryo, a rival operator controlled by Italy’s state-owned company Ferrovie dello Stato.
Wednesday’s collision occurred just before 9 a.m. local time, when a Renfe high-speed train hit an Iryo train between the villages of Los Yébenes and Urda, according to an official at Spain’s railway infrastructure manager Adif. The impact derailed at least two carriages on the Iryo train, interrupting all traffic on the high-speed line between Madrid and Seville.
Local authorities quickly dispatched ambulances, helicopters, police and Red Cross personnel, while the Spanish government deployed the army’s Emergency Military Unit, a special task force for civilian disasters and accidents.
Several trains are now halted as Adif helps travelers reach stations.
A spokesperson for Spain’s Transportation Ministry said the initial assessment suggests human error, potentially by an Adif rail traffic controller, was to blame. The Adif official declined to comment on what might have caused the accident.
The crash is likely to become a major talking point in Spain’s upcoming national election on Nov. 29. Sanchez and several ministers canceled their appointments for the day, as did the opposition leader.
Even before the cause or death toll was known, Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party, blamed the accident on the “abandonment, ruin and betrayal suffered by Spaniards” at the hands of Sánchez’s government.
Vox is polling third and could play a decisive role in forming the next government, with polls showing the conservative People’s Party in the lead.
Spain’s last major railway accident sparked a nationwide debate over the safety of the country’s nearly 4,000 kilometers of high-speed rail network, the world’s second-largest, according to the International Union of Railways.
That incident remains under investigation, but the opposition blames the government for neglecting infrastructure, from railways to roads.
Some 40 million people traveled on Spain’s commercial high-speed rail services in 2024, up 77% from 2019, according to data from the national competition authority. The increase partly reflects population growth as well as a surge in tourism, with Spain now receiving close to 100 million visitors a year.

Cost-of-living crisis
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is vulnerable to external energy shocks.
Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year.
The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget.
On Wednesday, Healey said he would deliver "breathing space" for families, saying the country needs "radical change on energy," and citing the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war — a conflict he said "we did not want."
His measures included the removal of standing charges on household gas heating bills, the extension of a tax break on electricity for millions of households through July 2027, and £100 ($133) checks for those living in the four lowest local housing tax bands. This will cost £2.6 billion.

Small business relief from business rates — a tax on commercial premises — would be extended to include more companies in the hospitality, retail and leisure sectors. The U.K.'s minimum wage will rise by 3.9%, while a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled.

XLE’s Price Has Surged, but Its Dividend Barely Moved
XLE has handed shareholders a stunning rally, but income investors buying in today are getting a very different deal than those who bought a year ago. The question is whether the fund's payout can keep up with its price.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Shares of the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSEARCA:XLE) have climbed 57% over the past year. Over the same stretch, the cash the fund pays out grew about 6%. For a retiree, that gap matters more than the rally. XLE holds only energy stocks in the S&P 500, weighted by market value, so its income comes from cash-rich producers.
The trailing yield has fallen to about 2.4%, down from around 3.4% on last year’s payout at last year’s price. The payouts look safe. Each dollar invested today simply buys much less income.
Where XLE’s Quarterly Checks Come From
XLE pays quarterly and passes through ordinary dividends from its holdings. The income comes entirely from what oil producers, refiners, and pipeline companies choose to pay.
Older records can look alarming because XLE completed a 2-for-1 forward split effective December 5, 2025. That explains why the September 2025 distribution of $0.75 looks twice the size of the $0.37 paid in December. On a split-adjusted basis, trailing-year distributions reached $1.52 per share, up from $1.44 the year before.
The fund is concentrated. Its most recent holdings filing is dated June 30, so the weights may have changed since then. That filing shows net assets of $35.7 billion, with Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) at 23% and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) at 16%. In practice, these two companies largely determine how safe XLE’s income is.
Big Oil Pays the Bills, and Coverage Holds
Exxon Mobil yields 2.2%. Its $4.08 annual dividend uses about 52% of trailing EPS of $7.83. That leaves plenty of room if oil prices fall back.
Chevron is the least certain pick among the oil producers. It yields 3.0%, but its $6.98 dividend takes about 67% of earnings, and those earnings come from a period of high oil prices. Coverage holds today, but a return to weaker crude would test it first.
Carrying a 7% weight, ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP) yields 2.2%. Its payout uses only about 44% of earnings, the largest buffer in the group.
Williams Companies (NYSE:WMB), a 5% position, yields 2.9%. Its dividend is 79% of GAAP (standard accounting) earnings, which looks tight. GAAP earnings understate a pipeline company’s cash, though, because they subtract large depreciation charges. The better test is distributable cash flow, meaning the cash left after maintenance spending, and the per-share earnings used here are only a conservative stand-in for it. Williams also takes in mostly fee-based revenue for moving gas, which shelters it from swings in commodity prices.
Commodity prices are the real risk to this income. Benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude recently traded near $108 a barrel, up 68% from a year ago. The low was $55 as recently as last December.

Bank of America's top technical strategist flagged a pattern that preceded every major market peak since 2000, and it is showing up again right now in the data investors use least.
At the end of September, Americans who borrow against their stocks owed their brokers about $1.48 trillion, close to a record. That debt has held up, but its growth has slowed sharply.
In a note dated October 23, 2026, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC | BAC Price Prediction) technical strategist Paul Ciana said year-over-year margin debt growth fell to 31.4% in September, down from 53.7% in May. He said that when growth cools off after an extreme run, the slowdown has lined up with past market peaks and can signal a top. He framed the slowdown as a warning sign of elevated risk.
Both the broad market and the retail broker rose after the warning. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) rose 0.57% to 769.66 on October 27. Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) gained 1.85% to $94.56 on the same day it reported a record margin book that is growing much more slowly.
Why BofA Pays Attention to Slowing Growth
BofA ranked May’s growth rate fourth-highest since 1998. The only higher levels came in 2000, 2007 and 2021, and a stock decline followed each one.
The total itself is still rising. September balances rose 1.80% from August and sit 1.47% below June’s high. The growth rate, however, has fallen.
The pace matters more than the total because each new dollar of margin debt is new buying power. When that new borrowing slows, the market loses a source of demand. If prices then fall, margin calls (demands from brokers for more cash or collateral) push borrowers to sell into the decline. Riding a late-cycle rally is fine as long as the exit is planned, which is the whole subject of our free bubble survivor’s handbook.
Ciana raised this risk before. On June 29, with growth near 54%, he wrote that “U.S. equities could face a corrective phase in the third quarter.” He also pointed to an opposing pattern: “Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize.”
Leverage Is Moving Into Funds and Options
Over one month, the ten largest leveraged equity ETFs took in $12 billion of new money while their market value fell $20 billion. The largest triple-leveraged semiconductor fund drew $9 billion in two weeks, the biggest two-week inflow in its history.

Options work the same way, because a small premium controls a large position. Retail traders recently made up 61% of options volume on one large market maker’s platform.

On a rainy Saturday in June 2024, Hannah Zarzecki cried as she crossed the Grandma’s Marathon finish line. It was her eighth marathon, and despite following a training plan, she didn’t achieve her sub-4 goal—again. “I kept telling myself, ‘Why did I sign up for this? I still can’t PR. I’m freezing cold. My feet hurt,’” she says. “It was so miserable.”
She didn’t know that a chance encounter at that race was about to change that.
A high school cross-country runner, Zarzecki returned to the sport after graduating from Harvard University, where she played ice hockey. Wanting a goal to work toward, she entered the 2018 Chicago Marathon lottery and won a bib in her hometown race.
Leading up to the race, Zarzecki had not run more than about 15 miles and didn’t follow a training plan. She was in good shape from teaching spin classes several nights a week and wasn’t sure how else to prepare. I’m either gonna finish this marathon, or I am gonna end up in the hospital, she remembers thinking. She was surprised and proud when, taking walk breaks, she ran her way to the finish in 5:04:59.
Not convinced that marathons were for her, Zarzecki turned her focus to shorter distances, 10Ks and half marathons—until a spin class student told her about completing the Berlin Marathon. She loved the idea of traveling to run races in other countries, so she applied for and got into the same marathon. After loosely following a training plan she found online this time, she ran and walked the 2021 Berlin Marathon in 5:16:32. Disappointed, she decided to commit to working on her time.
Zarzecki found a coach on Instagram whom she paid to create a training plan for her. She devoted herself to this regimen, which included her first experience with speedwork and intervals. She also joined the Electric Athletic Club in Chicago and participated in their group runs.
Zarzecki raced the 2022 Rock ’n’ Roll Nashville Marathon. Without taking walking breaks, she finished in 4:12:11, improving her Berlin time by more than an hour seven months later. “When I actually put my mind to training and following this plan, everything kind of came together, and I’m like, ‘Oh, this is how you’re supposed to do a marathon,’” she says. She was hooked.
For the next couple of years, Zarzecki used the same training plan, running about 30 miles each week. In May 2023, she surprised herself on her 28th birthday when she finished the Wisconsin Marathon in 4:00:28.
After that, her one goal became to break four hours. In the fall of 2023, she ran the Berlin Marathon followed by the Chicago Marathon two weeks later, finishing in 4:11:26 and 4:01:23, respectively. She came so close again yet couldn’t reach the elusive goal. When she finished the 2024 Grandma’s Marathon about eight minutes slower than her Chicago time, Zarzecki was in tears.
But Grandma’s was pivotal for a different reason. After the race, Zarzecki began talking with two female runners while she waited for her boyfriend to return with their car. They commiserated about the race and bad weather. The other two runners were trying to book a rideshare but were having no luck, so they asked if it would be possible to get a ride to the airport with Zarzecki. She and her boyfriend agreed even though it added 40 minutes to their return drive to Chicago. After Zarzecki refused compensation, one of the runners, a New York Road Runners coach, Maria Romano, suggested payment in kind: she would train Zarzecki for her next marathon.

Jon Mott set his marathon PR—a 2:17:20—on the famously flat and speedy course of the Berlin Marathon in 2022. Then, a few months later, he traveled to Boston for 26.2, feeling equally confident in his training, but was punished by the repeated hills and fell well short of his goal.
So what happened in Boston?
“At no point was I able to lock into my rhythm,” says Mott, a three-time U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier and run coach at Runnersfix. “There was no flow to the race, I guess you can say, and it just really beat me up.”
Over time, Mott came to see a pattern in his contrasting performances. On flat, rhythmic courses, he could open up his stride and cruise, letting his powerful gait carry him through the finish line with little interruption. But on hilly courses, he noticed runners, who could more easily shorten their stride and adjust their turnover, often seemed better equipped to handle the change of pace that comes with an undulating course.
Mott now uses this observation as a coaching lens with the runners he trains. He sees some athletes as more stride-oriented—like himself—and others as more cadence-oriented.
These designations aren’t fixed labels or an automatic explanation for every race result, but they offer a clue into a runner’s strengths and weaknesses. Generally, stride runners excel on flat courses but need more hill-specific preparation, while cadence runners tend to handle hills well but need more practice on flat terrain.
Here’s how to identify the pattern in your own running, why knowing your tendency could help you run your next race faster, and how to use this finding to prepare more intentionally for your next race.
Stride vs. Cadence Runner: What’s the Difference?
In Mott’s framework, stride runners succeed at fast paces by lengthening their stride while keeping their cadence relatively steady across all speeds. Cadence runners get faster mainly by taking more steps per minute, with a less pronounced change in stride length.
Mott first came across this distinction a few years ago while looking for a new racing shoe and comparing the 2024 edition of Asics’s Metaspeed Edge and Sky models. Drawing on data from its sports-science institute, Asics separated runners who primarily lengthen their stride as they speed up from those who primarily increase their step rate, Runner’s World previously reported. The company also found that stride runners tended to land closer to the midfoot or forefoot, while cadence runners more often had smoother turnover and favored more of a heel strike.
This helped Mott confirm the patterns he had noticed in his own races, and then he expanded that idea into his clients’ plans, using it to help figure out their strengths and where they might need more practice.
“Stride-dominant runners tend to rely more on stride length to generate speed,” Mott says. “But when running uphill, trying to maintain that longer stride can become inefficient and more demanding.” This explains why he felt so comfortable in Berlin—and why a hilly race such as Boston felt so difficult.
Cadence runners, in Mott’s view, flourish on courses with frequent changes in terrain. Because they rely more on step frequency to get faster, Mott believes they can more readily adjust their turnover. Essentially, their shorter, quicker steps make it easier to adapt to changes when the course may disrupt those with longer strides, he says.
